nameStory: The lime gall mite gets its name from its favorite host - lime trees (also called basswood or linden trees). These tiny mites create distinctive galls, which are abnormal growths that look like little bumps or blisters on leaves where the mites live and feed.
description: Lime gall mites are microscopic arachnids so tiny you'll never see the actual mite with your naked eye - they're smaller than a pinhead! Instead, you'll notice their handiwork: small, rounded bumps or blisters on lime tree leaves. These cream-colored to reddish galls are where entire colonies of mites live, feed, and reproduce. Each gall might house dozens of these nearly invisible creatures.

idTips.label: Gall Appearance
idTips.description: Look for small, dome-shaped bumps on the upper surface of lime tree leaves that feel slightly raised and firm to the touch, like tiny blisters

idTips.label: Host Plant
idTips.description: Only found on American basswood (lime) trees - look for heart-shaped leaves with serrated edges and asymmetrical bases

idTips.label: Gall Color
idTips.description: Fresh galls start pale green or cream-colored, gradually turning reddish-brown or tan as they mature and age

idTips.label: Gall Texture
idTips.description: Galls feel smooth and slightly waxy when you run your finger over them, distinctly different from the soft leaf tissue around them

idTips.label: Distribution Pattern
idTips.description: Multiple small galls scattered across individual leaves, often concentrated along the leaf veins where mites first settle

habitat: Found wherever American basswood trees grow in New England, from rich bottomland forests to mixed hardwood slopes. These mites prefer mature basswood trees in partially shaded areas, often in moist, well-drained soils typical of river valleys and protected woodland sites.

seasonality.spring: Adult mites emerge and begin forming new galls on fresh basswood leaves. Look for tiny, pale green bumps just starting to develop on young leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak gall development occurs with mature, prominent reddish-brown galls clearly visible on basswood leaves. This is the easiest time to spot their signs.
seasonality.fall: Galls become darker and more weathered as leaves begin to change color. Mites prepare to overwinter in bark crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adult mites hide in protected spots under loose bark scales of basswood trees. No galls visible since leaves have fallen.

funFact: These microscopic mites are so specialized that they can only complete their entire life cycle on one specific type of tree - if you moved them to any other plant species, even closely related trees, the entire colony would die!
confusionNotes: Lime gall mites create much smaller, more numerous galls than other leaf gall-makers like aphids or wasps. Remember: if the bumps are tiny (pencil eraser size or smaller) and only on basswood trees, you've found mite galls.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse 'lime trees' with citrus limes - in New England, lime trees refer to American basswood (Tilia americana), also called linden trees. These are large native shade trees with heart-shaped leaves, completely unrelated to citrus fruits.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives that create felt-like patches (Lime Felt Gall Mite) or target fruit trees (Pearleaf Blister Mite), the lime gall mite creates distinct raised bumps specifically on basswood leaves. Other Eriophyes species in the region typically cause different symptoms like leaf curling, nail-shaped projections, or fuzzy felt patches rather than these smooth, dome-shaped galls.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates elongated, finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that forms reddish blisters on fruit trees, the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite creates distinctly rounded, bump-like galls.

Red Nail Gall Mites create the most dramatically shaped galls in their genus - while relatives like the Lime Felt Gall Mite create fuzzy patches and others make simple bumps or blisters, only tiliae produces these unmistakable nail or horn-shaped protrusions.
Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates short, nail-like bumps on linden trees, the Plum Finger Gall Mite makes much longer, more cylindrical projections.

While many Eriophyes species create galls on different trees, the Alder Leaf Gall Mite's small, simple dome-shaped galls are quite different from relatives like the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that causes broad, blistered areas rather than distinct bumps.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-shaped galls on linden trees or finger-like projections on cherry leaves, the Birch Leaf Gall Mite creates relatively simple bumps and fuzzy patches.
Eriophyes rhoinus differs from its relatives primarily by its host plant preference for sumac species, while other Eriophyes mites specialize on different trees like cherry, maple, or alder.

While many Eriophyes mites in New England create galls on different trees, the Lime Felt Gall Mite is unique in producing that characteristic felt texture - its close relative the Red Nail Gall Mite makes hard, nail-like projections on linden leaves, while others like the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite create smooth pouches.
Unlike other Eriophyes species that target maples, cherries, or birches, this species is exclusively found on viburnums.
Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite that creates elongated finger-like projections, the Maple Gall Mite produces rounder, more dome-shaped galls.

Eriophyes leionotus differs from its relatives primarily by its specific host plant preferences and gall characteristics rather than the mite's appearance, since all Eriophyes species look remarkably similar under magnification.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-like projections (Red Nail Gall Mite) or finger-shaped growths (Plum Finger Gall Mite), the Serviceberry Gall Mite creates more subtle, pouch-like swellings.

Unlike other Eriophyes mites that create finger-like projections (like Plum Finger Gall Mite) or felt-like patches (like Lime Felt Gall Mite), the Pearleaf Blister Mite creates smooth, dome-shaped blisters.

Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite which creates smooth, nail-like projections, or the Lime Felt Gall Mite which makes dense, hair-like patches, this species creates more irregularly-shaped, moderately fuzzy galls.
